content_html:
Whether you're pricing a product for the first time or double-checking last quarter's numbers, a Profit Percentage Calculator tells you in seconds how much you actually earned relative to what something cost you. Enter two numbers and the tool applies the same ratio behind a profit calculator, a profit margin calculator, or a markup calculator — whatever name you know it by. Like other financial calculators, it turns raw numbers into a percentage instantly, but understanding the math behind it is what lets you use the result with confidence. This is one of the first ratios taught in business finance, because it needs nothing more than what you already have on an invoice.

How the Profit Percentage Calculator Works

It needs only two numbers: what you paid, and what you sold it for. Subtract one from the other to find your profit, then divide that profit by what you paid and multiply by 100. That single calculation is what separates this ratio from profit margin, which divides by the sale price instead — a distinction worth remembering before you compare the two results.

Cost Price, Selling Price, and Where the Percentage Comes From

Cost price (CP) is what you paid to acquire or produce an item — raw materials, wholesale cost, or your cost of goods sold (COGS) if you manufacture in bulk. It's effectively your unit cost per item. Selling price (SP) is what the customer actually pays; add SP up across every transaction and you get your revenue. The result sits between CP and SP: it's the gap between the two, expressed as a share of what you spent rather than what you charged. For a small business comparing quotes from two suppliers, that gap is the difference between a profitable order and a break-even one.

The Profit Percentage Formula in Plain Numbers

Written out, the formula breakdown looks like this:

$$\text{Profit} = SP - CP$$

$$\text{Profit \%} = \frac{\text{Profit}}{CP} \times 100$$

This is standard business mathematics, and it's exactly what this calculator automates for you. It's also different from a sales tax calculation, which adds a percentage on top of a price rather than measuring what you kept from it. If SP is lower than CP, the calculator returns a negative result — a loss amount instead of a profit — using the same math in reverse.

TermFormulaExample
ProfitSP − CP500 − 400 = 100
Profit %(Profit ÷ CP) × 100(100 ÷ 400) × 100 = 25%
Profit Margin(Profit ÷ SP) × 100(100 ÷ 500) × 100 = 20%
MarkupSame calculation, expressed against cost25%

Notice the two results from the exact same sale: a 25% figure measured against cost, but only a 20% profit margin measured against revenue. In accounting terms, neither number is wrong — they're just measured against different bases.

Profit Percentage vs. Profit Margin vs. Markup

These three words get used interchangeably in conversation, and the figure behind them is, at its core, a simple financial metric — but whether you're computing gross margin or markup, the base you divide by changes the result, and that matters when you're reading someone else's financial reporting.

Why Markup and Profit Margin Give Different Numbers

Markup is just another name for the same calculation, using cost as the base instead of revenue. It's always a bigger number than profit margin on a profitable sale, because it divides by the smaller cost rather than the larger of the two. Buy something for 400 and sell it for 500: markup is 25%, margin is 20%. The gap widens as the profit grows, so two businesses quoting different figures for the same deal could both be technically correct — always check which one you're looking at before comparing a result against industry standards.

Gross Profit Margin, Net Profit, and Net Profit Margin Explained

Gross profit margin only accounts for COGS — it ignores rent, salaries, and other overhead, and is sometimes marketed as a gross profit calculator when a tool is built purely to find that one figure. Net profit, by contrast, is what's left after every expense is subtracted from revenue — sometimes called net income — and net profit margin expresses that leftover income as a percentage of revenue. A healthy profit margin at the gross level doesn't guarantee one at the net level, which is exactly why a business's financial health is judged on more than one margin figure alone. This kind of profitability analysis is what turns a raw invoice into a decision about whether to keep selling at that price.

Worked Examples: Putting the Markup Calculator to the Test

Numbers stick better with real transactions attached to them. These profit and loss calculations rely on the exact same math covered above, applied to a plain markup, a loss, and a reverse target-profit calculation.

Retail Markup, a Loss, and a Reverse Target-Profit Calculation

  1. Markup example: A shop buys a jacket for 800 and sells it for 1,200. Profit = 400. Profit % = (400 ÷ 800) × 100 = 50% — for every unit of cost, the shop earns half a unit back in profit.
  2. Loss example: A phone bought for 6,000 is marked down and sold for 5,000 in a clearance sale. Loss = 1,000. Loss percentage = (1,000 ÷ 6,000) × 100 = 16.67%, since the sale price fell below cost.
  3. Target profit example: A baker's cost per cake is 120, and she has a target profit of 40% (0.4 as a decimal). Selling price = 120 × (1 + 40 ÷ 100) = 168, giving a profit of 48 per cake.

How to Calculate Profit Percentage for Target Pricing

Sometimes you're not checking a past sale — you're setting a future price. If you already know your cost and the percentage you want to hit, you can calculate profit percentage in reverse to find what to charge. Target pricing is really just a pricing strategy in reverse: decide the number first, then solve for the price that gets you there.

The Profit Margin Formula for Setting a Price

Switch the profit percentage formula around and solve for SP instead of profit: SP = CP × (1 + Profit% ÷ 100). This mode is what you reach for when you're quoting a client, drafting a quote for a supplier order, or simply making sure a discount you're about to offer still leaves your desired margin intact.

Tip: if you already know the price you need to match, run the calculator the other way and solve for cost instead — useful when negotiating with a vendor before you commit to a purchase price.

Cost of Goods Sold, Gross Margin, and What Else a Profit Margin Calculator Should Account For

A calculator built only around two raw numbers is a good start, but COGS, gross margin, and a handful of related expenses all shape whether that percentage reflects real profitability, not just a partial picture.

Operating Expenses, Taxes, and What Shrinks Your Bottom Line

That gross-level number only strips out COGS. Net margin goes further, subtracting operating expenses, interest, and taxes as well — which is why two products with an identical result at the register can end up with very different bottom lines once rent, labor costs, and debt payments are factored in. Larger businesses sometimes track a step further with EBITDA margin — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization — and EBITDA itself shows up often in company financial statements as a proxy for operating profitability before financing decisions muddy the picture. If you're also watching how long your reserves will last while you get there, a cash burn rate calculation alongside this number tells you that story too.

How to Raise Your Margin When the Numbers Fall Short

If your margin is lower than you'd like, the fix is usually on one of two sides of the formula: raise the price, or lower the cost.

  • Increase average order value through upselling and cross-selling instead of only chasing more sales.
  • Negotiate better terms with vendors before accepting their first quote.
  • Audit recurring operating costs and labor costs — unused subscriptions, idle tools, and overstaffed shifts quietly erode your margin every month.
  • Avoid discounting reflexively; every discount you offer lowers your result on that sale.

Margin Outside Everyday Pricing: What a Margin Calculator Reveals About Stock Trading and Currency Exchange

This kind of percentage math isn't only a retail concept. The word margin shows up just as often in stock trading and currency exchange, though there it means something closer to collateral than to profit.

Margin Trading, Margin Requirements, and Security Deposits

In margin trading, a broker lets you borrow money to buy more securities than your cash alone would cover. The margin requirement is the percentage of the purchase price you must put up yourself — often treated like a security deposit that protects the broker if the trade moves against you. A 25% margin requirement, for instance, lets you control four times as much stock as the cash you've deposited.

Currency Exchange Margin and Exchange Rates

Currency exchange margin works similarly: it's the deposit you maintain to hold an open position while trading one currency against another at a given exchange rate. None of this changes the underlying formula from earlier in this article — it's the same ratio of gain to what you put at risk, just applied to a different kind of transaction. Whatever your business structure or industry, the same logic applies: figure out what you put in, what you got out, and divide accordingly.
